197.title: Contentment is wealth (201–204)
197.hook: victory breeds hatred; health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth (Dhammapada 204)
197.howItsDone: Contentment with little is one of the qualities Buddhist monastics are trained in, and lay Buddhists often quote verse 204 as everyday wisdom about health, enough and trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, among those who hate: happy among the hating, fed by joy with an empty bowl. Your line was we live happily. Did you stay steady in one sour room? Day one hundred ninety-seven.

You get the raise. For about two weeks it feels wonderful. Then the new number becomes the normal number, and you start noticing what the next one would buy. Or you win the argument, and the other person goes quiet, and somehow the room feels worse than before. Everyone has chased a finish line that kept moving. There's a word for being able to stop at the line you're already standing on, and today's verse calls it the best kind of money there is. Today: contentment is wealth.
screen: `THE RAISE FEELS GREAT FOR TWO WEEKS.` → `YOU WIN, AND THE ROOM FEELS WORSE.` → `A FINISH LINE THAT KEEPS MOVING.`

segments.voice: Verse two oh one, in Max Müller's words: "Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy." The commentary says the Buddha spoke it after King Pasenadi of Kosala lost a battle to his own nephew and couldn't eat or sleep for shame. Winning makes an enemy; losing makes you miserable. The only way out of that seesaw is to step off it. Then the chapter's great list, verse two oh four: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness." The Pali for contentment is santuṭṭhi, being satisfied with what's there. It isn't laziness, and it isn't giving up on improving things. It's the ability to stop feeling poor when you have enough. And there's a lovely story behind that verse too. The same King Pasenadi, the commentary says, ate so much at every meal that he could barely stay awake to hear the Buddha teach. The Buddha suggested he eat a little less, mindfully. The king had his nephew recite a short verse at every meal as a reminder, cut back bit by bit, grew slim and well, and came back to thank him. Health, the greatest gift. Notice where the list ends: trust as the best kind of kinship, and nibbāna, the deepest ease, as the highest happiness. Every item on it is something you can't buy, which is exactly the point.
screen: `VICTORY BREEDS HATRED.` · `STEP OFF THE SEESAW.` · `SANTUṬṬHI — ENOUGH.` · `A KING WHO ATE TOO MUCH.` · then, large: `CONTENTMENT IS WEALTH.`

segments.voice: Sit, and name, slowly, three things in your life that are already enough. Not perfect: enough. Maybe the bed you slept in. A pair of shoes that fit. One person who would pick up if you called. As you name each one, let the breath out a little longer, the way you'd sigh after a good meal. Notice any voice that says yes, but. Let it talk, and don't follow it. Just stay with the three enoughs, and then with the breath, which is also enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Contentment is wealth. Verse two oh four: health is the greatest gift, contentment the best riches, trust the best kinship, nibbāna the highest happiness.
Your line: contentment is wealth. Today, the next time you catch yourself wanting the next thing, name one thing you already have that is enough. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

198.title: Good company (205–208)
198.hook: to see the noble is good; follow the wise as the moon follows the path of the stars
198.howItsDone: Buddhists place great weight on kalyāṇamitta, good spiritual friendship, through teachers, the monastic community and fellow practitioners, and many see visiting a respected monk or nun as a blessing in itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, contentment is wealth: health the greatest gift, enough the best riches. Your line was contentment is wealth. What did you name as already enough? Day one hundred ninety-eight.

Think of someone you always feel a little better after seeing. Not because they flatter you. Maybe they're just steady. They listen all the way to the end of your sentence. They don't gossip, and somehow around them you don't either. You leave the coffee with them standing a bit straighter. Now think of someone who has the opposite effect. You know exactly who. We become, slowly, like the people we spend our hours with. Chapter fifteen ends with that simple and slightly uncomfortable truth. Today: good company.
screen: `SOMEONE YOU FEEL BETTER AFTER SEEING.` → `AND SOMEONE WHO'S THE OPPOSITE.` → `WE BECOME OUR COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Verse two oh six, in Max Müller's translation: "The sight of the elect (Arya) is good, to live with them is always happiness". Ariya means noble, not by birth but by character: someone well along the path. Just seeing such a person, the verse says, is good. Then verse two oh seven: "company with the wise is pleasure, like meeting with kinsfolk." Like coming home to family. And the closing image, verse two oh eight: "one ought to follow a good and wise man, as the moon follows the path of the stars." In old India, the moon's path through the sky was traced along a ring of star groups, the lunar mansions. The moon doesn't wander at random; it keeps to a known road. Good friends are that road. The Buddha put this more strongly than you might expect. In one discourse, his attendant Ānanda says that good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrects him: not half. It's the whole of the holy life. The Pali phrase is kalyāṇamitta, a lovely friend, a good friend, someone whose company leans you toward the good. The verses also say that time with fools is painful, and that's worth reading carefully. Buddhists don't take it as permission to look down on anyone. It's about whose habits you're soaking in, day after day, and choosing on purpose. Because you will soak something in. The only question is what.
screen: `ARIYA — NOBLE BY CHARACTER.` · `LIKE MEETING FAMILY.` · `THE MOON FOLLOWS THE STARS.` · `NOT HALF: THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `KEEP GOOD COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one good person in your life. Not perfect: good. Someone whose company leans you toward patience or honesty or kindness. Picture their face, the way they sound. Let yourself feel glad they exist. If you like, silently wish them well: may you be happy, may you be safe. Then ask one small question: when could I spend a little time with them this week? A call, a walk, a message. Hold that plan lightly, and rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Good company. Verse two oh eight: follow the good and the wise, as the moon follows the path of the stars.
Your line: keep good company. Today, spend a few minutes with a good person, in person or on the phone, and notice how you feel afterward. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

199.title: From the dear, grief (209–216)
199.hook: from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear; one free of it has neither
199.howItsDone: Monastic Buddhists practice letting go of close attachments, while lay Buddhists often understand these verses as a call to love without clinging, and to meet loss with the understanding that everything dear will change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, good company: follow the wise, as the moon follows the stars. Your line was keep good company. Who did you spend a few minutes with? Day one hundred ninety-nine, and chapter sixteen begins.

You don't worry about a stranger's phone falling in the lake. You don't lie awake over a coworker's cousin's surgery. But your own kid is ten minutes late, and your stomach starts to knot. Your dog limps, and the whole evening goes gray. The things we love are exactly the things that can hurt us. Everyone who has ever loved anything knows this, and most of us decide it's worth it. Chapter sixteen of the Dhammapada looks at that trade with unusual honesty. Today: from the dear, grief.
screen: `A STRANGER'S PHONE IN THE LAKE.` → `YOUR KID, TEN MINUTES LATE.` → `WHAT WE LOVE CAN HURT US.`

segments.voice: Chapter sixteen is called Piyavagga. Piya means dear, beloved, precious. Müller titled it pleasure, but dear is closer. Verse two twelve, in his words: "From pleasure comes grief, from pleasure comes fear; he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear." In Pali it's: from what is dear comes sorrow, from what is dear comes fear. Then the verse repeats with other words: from affection, from lust, from love, from craving. Five times, the same shape. There's a story in the Udāna, one of the early collections. Visākhā, one of the Buddha's greatest lay supporters, came to him in wet clothes and wet hair, grieving a grandchild who had died. He asked her: would you like as many children and grandchildren as there are people in this city? Yes, she said. And how many people die in this city each day? Many, she said. Then, he answered gently, you'd never be without wet clothes and wet hair. Those who have a hundred dear ones have a hundred sorrows. Those who have none have none. This is hard teaching, and Buddhists read it in more than one way. Monastics take it literally, as a reason to let go of close ties. Many lay teachers read it as being about grasping, not love: you can love fully, and still hold loosely, knowing that everything dear will change. The tradition's own loving-kindness, metta, wishes all beings well without clutching any of them. The verses don't forbid love. They tell the truth about its cost.
screen: `PIYA — DEAR, BELOVED.` · `FIVE TIMES, THE SAME SHAPE.` · `VISĀKHĀ IN WET CLOTHES.` · `LOVE FULLY, HOLD LOOSELY.` · then, large: `FROM THE DEAR, GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one person, animal or thing you love. Let yourself feel the love, warmly, fully. Then notice whether there's a small grip in it too: a tightness, a fear of losing it. Don't push the love away. Just soften the grip, the way you'd open a fist that was holding a bird too tightly. Wish them well: may you be safe, may you be at ease, whatever happens. Love without clutching. Then rest in the breath, open-handed. The bell holds the time.
From the dear. Verse two twelve: from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear; one who is free of it knows neither.
Your line: from the dear, grief. Today, love one thing without grasping: enjoy it fully, and let it be free to change. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

200.title: Welcomed home (217–220)
200.hook: as kin welcome a traveler home, good deeds welcome the one who did good
200.howItsDone: Many Buddhists make merit through giving, keeping precepts and practice, and often dedicate that merit to others; these verses are commonly cited to describe good deeds as what goes with a person beyond this life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, from the dear: from what is dear comes grief, and Visākhā in wet clothes. Your line was from the dear, grief. What did you love without grasping? Day two hundred. That's a real number. Well walked.

Picture the arrivals gate at an airport. The doors slide open, and someone walks out after a long time away: a soldier, a student back from a year abroad, a grandmother who flew halfway around the world. And there's a little crowd waiting. Balloons, a handmade sign, a kid who breaks loose and runs. Nobody at that gate is thinking about the traveler's résumé. They're just glad. Everyone knows what it feels like to be welcomed home like that, or wishes they did. Today's verse takes that gate and puts it somewhere unexpected. Today: welcomed home.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS GATE.` → `A SIGN, BALLOONS, A KID WHO RUNS.` → `THE GATE, SOMEWHERE UNEXPECTED.`

segments.voice: Chapter sixteen has spent its first verses on the grief that comes from what is dear. It ends by turning to what is dear in a good way. Verse two seventeen, in Max Müller's words, describes a person the world holds dear: one with virtue and insight, who is just, speaks the truth, and "does what is his own business". Then the two verses the outline is named for. Verse two nineteen: "Kinsmen, friends, and lovers salute a man who has been long away, and returns safe from afar." And verse two twenty: "In like manner his good works receive him who has done good, and has gone from this world to the other;--as kinsmen receive a friend on his return." The Pali word for those good works is puñña, often translated merit: goodness that builds up, like savings. In Buddhist teaching, a person continues after death according to their actions, and here the actions themselves are pictured as family at the gate. The old commentary gives it a story. A generous man named Nandiya built a hall for the monks. The great disciple Moggallāna, the story says, visited a heaven realm and saw a mansion already being prepared there for Nandiya, before Nandiya had even died. You don't have to picture heaven to feel what this is saying. Every kind thing you do is, in a sense, sent ahead. It goes on before you. And one day you catch up with it, and it's waiting at the gate with a handmade sign.
screen: `WHAT IS DEAR, IN A GOOD WAY.` · `KIN AT THE GATE.` · `PUÑÑA — GOODNESS THAT BUILDS UP.` · `NANDIYA'S MANSION, AHEAD OF HIM.` · then, large: `GOOD DEEDS GREET YOU.`

segments.voice: Sit, and imagine yourself a year from now, coming home after a long day. What small good thing could you do today that future you would be glad to find waiting? A drawer cleared. A letter written. A friendship tended. A debt paid. Money set aside for someone who needs it. Pick one. Picture future you finding it, and feeling welcomed. Then let the picture go, and rest in the breath, here, with nothing to do but this. The bell holds the time.
Welcomed home. Verse two twenty: as kin welcome a traveler returning, good deeds welcome the one who did good.
Your line: good deeds greet you. Today, do the one good thing you picked, for your future self, and leave it waiting at the gate. Day two hundred.

201.title: Hold the chariot (221–222)
201.hook: one who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot is a real driver; others only hold the reins
201.howItsDone: Buddhists practice restraining anger as it arises, by noticing it in the body, pausing and breathing, and many recite the Buddha's title 'the incomparable trainer of those who can be tamed' in daily chanting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, welcomed home: good deeds waiting at the gate like family. Your line was good deeds greet you. What did you leave waiting for your future self? Day two hundred one, and chapter seventeen begins: anger.

Anyone can hold a steering wheel. On an empty road on a sunny day, everyone's a fine driver. The real test comes when a car cuts you off, or the road turns to ice, or the kid in the back seat spills the juice right as the light turns yellow. That's when you find out whether you're driving or just holding on. Anger works the same way. Everyone is patient when nothing is pushing. Chapter seventeen of the Dhammapada is about anger, and its second verse gives you the best job title in the book. Today: hold the chariot.
screen: `ANYONE CAN HOLD A WHEEL.` → `ICE, A CUT-OFF, SPILLED JUICE.` → `DRIVING, OR JUST HOLDING ON?`

segments.voice: The chapter opens with verse two twenty-one, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride, let him overcome all bondage!" Then comes the image. Verse two twenty-two: "He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins." Picture a chariot in the ancient world: horses at full gallop, wooden wheels, no brakes. Once it's rolling, stopping it takes real strength and skill. Anger, the verse says, is like that. It arises, gathers speed, and wants to run. Holding it back isn't the same as never feeling it. The chariot is already moving. The skill is in not letting it run over anyone. The Pali word for anger is kodha, and the verse's word for the real driver is sārathi, a charioteer: the same word Buddhists use in one of the Buddha's titles, the incomparable trainer of those who can be tamed. The old commentary gives the verse a surprising story. A monk, clearing ground for a hut, cut down a tree and injured the child of the spirit who lived in it. The tree spirit, furious, raised her hand to strike him. And then she stopped. She held it back. She went to the Buddha and told him, and he praised her with this very verse. A real driver isn't the one who never feels the horses pull. It's the one who feels them pull, hard, and still holds the chariot.
screen: `LEAVE ANGER, FORSAKE PRIDE.` · `A ROLLING CHARIOT, NO BRAKES.` · `FEELING IT ISN'T DRIVING IT.` · `THE TREE SPIRIT HOLDS BACK.` · then, large: `HOLD THE CHARIOT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and remember a small moment of anger from this week. Not the biggest one; a small one. Feel how it started: heat in the face, a tight jaw, words lining up. That's the chariot starting to roll. Now, in your mind, take the reins. Not by fighting the horses, just by leaning back, slowing, one breath at a time. Feel the speed come down. You're still the one in the chariot. You're just driving it now. Then let the scene go, and let the breath be the steady road. The bell holds the time.
Hold the chariot. Verse two twenty-two: one who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot is a real driver; the rest only hold the reins.
Your line: hold the chariot. Today, when you feel one flash of anger start to roll, lean back on the reins for three breaths before you say or do anything. Day two hundred one.

202.title: Overcome anger by kindness (223–228)
202.hook: overcome anger by not-anger, evil by good, the miser by giving, the liar by truth; no one is never blamed
202.howItsDone: Verse 223 is among the most quoted in Theravada teaching on patience, and Buddhists practice meeting hostility with calm and generosity, often supported by loving-kindness meditation toward difficult people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hold the chariot: a real driver holds back rising anger, the rest only hold the reins. Your line was hold the chariot. Did you lean back for three breaths? Day two hundred two.

Someone is rude to you at the checkout. The obvious move is to match them: a little coldness back, a sigh, maybe a comment. It feels fair. And then you both walk away a bit worse than you arrived. Now picture the other move. You say, it's been a long day for you, hasn't it, and smile. Sometimes the other person softens right there. Sometimes they don't. But something in you stays clean either way. Yesterday was about stopping the chariot. Today's verse is about which direction to drive it. Today: overcome anger by kindness.
screen: `RUDE AT THE CHECKOUT.` → `MATCH THEM, OR THE OTHER MOVE.` → `WHICH DIRECTION TO DRIVE.`

segments.voice: Verse two twenty-three, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!" Four pairs, and each one fights with the opposite weapon. Müller wrote love, but the Pali is akkodha, simply non-anger, calm. You don't beat anger by being angrier. You beat it by not joining in. The same with the rest: harm is met with good, stinginess with generosity, lies with truth. It's a strategy of opposites, and it only works if you refuse the other person's weapon. Then the chapter turns to something that makes all this easier: you'll be criticized no matter what. The commentary tells of a layman named Atula who went with friends to hear a teaching. The first monk they visited sat in silence, and Atula grumbled that he said nothing. The next, Sāriputta, gave a long, deep teaching, and Atula grumbled that it was too long. The next, Ānanda, spoke briefly, and he grumbled that it was too short. Finally he went to the Buddha, who told him, in verse two twenty-seven, that this was an old saying: they blame the silent, they blame the talkative, they blame the one who says little, "there is no one on earth who is not blamed." And verse two twenty-eight: "There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised." If blame is guaranteed, you're free. You might as well answer with kindness.
screen: `FOUR PAIRS OF OPPOSITES.` · `AKKODHA — NON-ANGER.` · `ATULA BLAMES EVERYONE.` · `NO ONE ESCAPES BLAME.` · then, large: `OVERCOME BY GIVING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone who has been harsh with you lately. Picture their face, as neutrally as you can. Notice the urge to match them. Now try the opposite weapon, just in your mind. For harshness, a kind word. For stinginess, a small gift. For a lie, a plain truth, gently said. Pick the one that fits. Picture yourself offering it. You don't have to do it today; just rehearse it. Then wish them ease for one breath, and let them go. The bell holds the time.
Overcome anger by kindness. Verse two twenty-three: anger by non-anger, harm by good, the stingy by giving, the liar by truth.
Your line: overcome by giving. Today, answer one piece of harshness with kindness, or one bit of stinginess with a small gift. Day two hundred two.

203.title: Three doors guarded (229–234)
203.hook: guard against anger of the body, of the tongue, of the mind
203.howItsDone: Buddhist ethics sorts action into three doors, body, speech and mind, and the ten wholesome courses of action (three of body, four of speech, three of mind) are a common framework for daily reflection and confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, overcome anger by kindness: four harms, four opposite weapons, and Atula, who blamed everyone. Your line was overcome by giving. What did you answer with kindness? Day two hundred three, the end of the week.

Think of a house with three doors. A front door, a back door, and a side door by the garage. You can lock the front door every night with great care, but if the side door is wide open, anyone can walk in. Anger is like a visitor who tries every door. Some of us guard our hands well: we'd never hit anyone. But the tongue is wide open. Or we're careful with words, and the mind is quietly running a whole courtroom drama in the background. Chapter seventeen ends by checking every door in the house. Today: three doors guarded.
screen: `A HOUSE WITH THREE DOORS.` → `THE FRONT LOCKED, THE SIDE OPEN.` → `ANGER TRIES EVERY DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, a picture of a person nobody could honestly blame: like a coin of gold from the Jambu river, praised even by the gods. And how do you become that? By guarding three doors. Verse two thirty-one, in Max Müller's translation: "Beware of bodily anger, and control thy body!" Verse two thirty-two: "Beware of the anger of the tongue, and control thy tongue!" And verse two thirty-three: "Beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind!" Each verse has the same two halves: stop the harm through that door, and use that same door for good. The body that could strike can also help. The tongue that could wound can also comfort. Then the chapter's last line, verse two thirty-four: "The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled." Buddhist teaching calls these the three doors of action: body, speech and mind, in Pali kāya, vacī and mano. Every action, it says, goes out through one of them. That's why the ten classic wholesome actions are sorted this way: three for the body, four for speech, and three for the mind. And notice which one is listed last. The mind is where anger first knocks, long before the tongue or the hand. Now look back at the whole week, a house with good doors. Contentment is wealth. Keep good company. From the dear, grief. Good deeds greet you. Hold the chariot. Overcome by giving. And today: three doors guarded.
screen: `A COIN OF JAMBU-RIVER GOLD.` · `BODY, TONGUE, MIND.` · `STOP THE HARM; USE THE DOOR WELL.` · `THE MIND IS WHERE IT KNOCKS FIRST.` · then, large: `THREE DOORS GUARDED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and check each door in turn. The body: notice your hands, your shoulders, your jaw. Is anything clenched? Let it soften. Then the tongue: is there a sharp sentence waiting behind your teeth for someone today? Let it rest there, unspoken. Then the mind: is there an argument running in the background? Just notice it, and let it quiet down on the out-breath. Three doors, all gently closed to anger, and all open to kindness. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Three doors guarded. Verses two thirty-one to two thirty-four: guard against anger of the body, of the tongue and of the mind, and use each for good.
Your line: three doors guarded. Today, guard your speech especially: before one sharp sentence leaves, check the door. Day two hundred three.

match.prompt: match each door to its Pali name.

myth: the verses only ask you to stop harm through each door
each also says to use that same door for good.
the ten wholesome actions are sorted by the three doors
three of body, four of speech, three of mind.
verse 234 lists the mind last
body, tongue, then mind: and the mind is where anger first knocks.

fork.setup: you'd never hit anyone, and you're careful with words. but in your head you've been arguing with a coworker all morning. which door is open?
fork.reveal: verse 233: "beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind!" the mind is the door anger tries first.

original.note: Pali: a door or gate — the teaching of the three doors of action (kāya, vacī, mano) uses this word.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't lose your temper.
what it means: anger can come out through the body, the tongue or the mind, so guard all three, and use each door for good.
what a scholar hears: the kammadvāra, the three doors of action, organize the ten kusala kammapatha; the verses themselves name body, tongue and mind.
